question: How broadly is task-relevant information dispersed across coordinates of pre-trained neural representations, which training and architecture choices govern that dispersion, and can random coordinate subsets support efficient downstream transfer without disproportionate class-level harm?

key_findings.claim: Random coordinate subsets of sufficiently wide pre-trained representations often retain much of the full representation's linear-probe accuracy across the tested vision tasks.
key_findings.evidence: The abstract reports that 20% of a standard ImageNet-1k ResNet50 penultimate layer gives CIFAR-10 accuracy within 5% of the full-layer probe. Table 1 reports, at a relative-performance tolerance of 0.9, that 70-95% of coordinates can be discarded on CIFAR-10 for the six tested architectures, while the discardable fraction varies substantially by architecture and task. Figures 1 and 4-7 extend the curve-level observation across standard and adversarial training, CNNs, ViTs, upstream datasets, layer widths, and MRL models.

key_findings.claim: The proposed DR score is a useful task-relative threshold summary, but the reported estimator does not establish that almost every random subset works.
key_findings.evidence: Equation 1 defines DR as one minus the smallest retained fraction whose mean performance ratio over all masks of that size reaches delta. The exact average is exponential to compute, so the experiments evaluate only five random masks at each selected size. A mean criterion is not a lower quantile or high-probability guarantee and can be met by a mixture of strong and weak masks; five draws do not tightly estimate tail failure probability. The paper separately treats small sample standard deviation as evidence of diffusion, but supplies no confidence interval, mask-level success rate, or preregistered threshold grid.

anchors.section: Diffused redundancy hypothesis and evaluation protocol

key_findings.claim: High linear CKA between random parts and the whole supports shared sample geometry, but it does not by itself show that semantic features are replicated neuron by neuron.
key_findings.evidence: Figures 1 and 2 show rapidly rising CKA with subset size, low variation across random picks, and CKA around 0.8 between two 10% subsets for the adversarially trained ResNet50. Yet a coordinate subset is algebraically contained in the full representation, CKA is dominated by covariance geometry, and correlated or low-effective-rank coordinates can yield the same pattern without identifiable replicated features. No whitened/isotropic null, coordinate permutation control, feature-recovery test, or causal intervention distinguishes literal replication from anisotropy, superposition, or shared class structure.

key_findings.claim: Matching top-PCA linear-probe accuracy does not justify the paper's explanation that a random subset captures the maximum possible variance in k dimensions.
key_findings.evidence: Figure 2c-d compares downstream classification accuracy from k random coordinates with accuracy after projection onto the top k principal components. PCA maximizes unsupervised retained variance or reconstruction quality, not supervised linear-probe accuracy; two representations can have the same classification score while retaining very different variance and information. The paper never reports explained-variance ratios, subspace angles, covariance reconstruction, or label-signal alignment, so the proposed mechanism does not follow from the displayed metric.

key_findings.claim: The random-projection baseline is not a valid basis for concluding that coordinate sampling is a uniquely useful constrained projection.
key_findings.evidence: Figure 3's dense random projection remains far below coordinate sampling even when k equals the full 2,048-dimensional layer. At full dimension a nonsingular projection preserves exactly the set of linear classifiers, so any remaining accuracy gap reflects conditioning, optimization, or implementation rather than lost linear information. The paper says it samples a normalized Gaussian matrix, but the released implementation at the repository's pinned submodule commit 3c0e3dd constructs a column-normalized torch.rand matrix with entries in [0,1]; its positive, nonzero-mean columns are strongly aligned rather than an isotropic Gaussian projection. The same fixed learning rate and weight decay are then used without conditioning or orthogonalization controls.

key_findings.claim: The experiments indicate real task and pre-training dependence rather than one architecture-independent redundancy constant.
key_findings.evidence: Adversarially trained ImageNet-1k models usually need fewer retained coordinates than their standard counterparts; ViTs trained on ImageNet-21k usually dominate the corresponding ImageNet-1k curves; and CIFAR-100 and Flowers often need more coordinates than CIFAR-10 or Oxford-IIIT-Pets. Table 1 ranges from only 20% discardable for ResNet50 on Flowers to 95% for WideResNet50-2 or VGG16 on CIFAR-10 at delta=0.9. The study appropriately frames the useful dimension as a downstream-task-dependent frontier rather than a universal intrinsic dimension.

key_findings.claim: Reducing the trained penultimate width weakens the observed random-coordinate redundancy, although the comparison does not isolate width as a causal variable across matched training runs.
key_findings.evidence: Figure 6 compares ResNet50 variants with penultimate widths from 2,048 down to 8 and reports that the 8-coordinate model requires more than 90% of its representation to approach full-layer performance. The checkpoints are taken from the MRL release, but the paper gives no repeated pre-training seeds, matched full-model accuracy table, or factorial width-by-loss experiment. Relative-to-own-full-layer accuracy also changes the target when representation capacity and full accuracy differ, so the curves support association with width more strongly than an inevitability claim.

key_findings.claim: MRL provides a clearly structured low-dimensional option, while random coordinates from the same or ordinary wide models become competitive only after the extreme low-coordinate regime.
key_findings.evidence: Figure 7 compares the designated MRL prefixes with random subsets of the MRL representation and with standard and adversarial representations. The optimized prefix is best on the far-left portion of most curves, while random subsets catch up as more coordinates are retained. This supports the paper's practical distinction: random access reveals natural redundancy, whereas MRL tells a deployment system exactly which contiguous prefix to store and use at each budget.

key_findings.claim: The conclusion that dropout and DeCov have almost no effect on diffused redundancy is under-validated.
key_findings.evidence: Figures 21-22 show one family of curves for dropout strengths 0.1-0.8 and one DeCov coefficient of 1e-4 and visually similar DR thresholds. However, Appendix B documents the downloaded checkpoints and downstream probes but gives no upstream optimizer, schedule, augmentation, model seed, top-1 accuracy, or training variance for the nine newly trained regularized models. There is one DeCov strength, no direct covariance/effective-rank measurement showing that it successfully decorrelated the evaluated layer, and no statistical equivalence test. A null effect on five-mask probe curves therefore cannot establish that decorrelation leaves redundancy unchanged or that the phenomenon is inevitable.

key_findings.claim: Dropping coordinates is associated with larger class-accuracy dispersion, but the paper's fairness interpretation and prediction-homogeneity claim exceed the measurements.
key_findings.evidence: Figure 8 and Appendix Figure 10 show Gini and coefficient-of-variation values increasing as mean accuracy decreases. These statistics are computed over label classes, not protected or socially salient groups, and part of their increase is mechanically coupled to the falling bounded mean. Figures 11-13 are heatmaps of class-wise accuracies; they do not show predicted-label distributions, confusion matrices, or error destinations, so they cannot establish the captions' claim of nearly homogeneous predictions. There are no uncertainty bars, matched-accuracy intervention, subgroup labels, or fairness criterion such as equalized opportunity.

key_findings.claim: The paper demonstrates feature-storage and linear-probe savings, not end-to-end inference or energy efficiency.
key_findings.evidence: Every experiment freezes and runs the full pre-trained backbone, then replaces only the downstream linear probe's input with selected coordinates. No FLOPs, wall-clock latency, memory traffic, feature-extraction time, compiled channel pruning, energy, or retraining cost is measured. Unless selected output rows can be computed without the rest of the backbone and its penultimate transformation, random-coordinate selection does not remove the layer or accelerate most inference. The conclusion's reduced training-time and green-AI benefits therefore remain plausible deployment hypotheses rather than evaluated outcomes.

key_findings.claim: The direct evidence base is broad in model count but shallow in independent pre-training and mask replication.
key_findings.evidence: The paper reports 30 model variants and four main downstream datasets, plus ImageNet-1k, ImageNetV2, and Places365 checks. Most variants are single downloaded checkpoints, the newly trained dropout/DeCov variants lack repeated upstream seeds, and each DR point uses five masks; the pairwise CKA experiment uses ten pairs. No across-checkpoint uncertainty, multiple-comparison correction, calibration split for delta, or confidence bound on the critical fraction is reported.

key_findings.claim: The intermediate-layer extension is not reproducible enough to support the paper's claim that the phenomenon applies to any layer.
key_findings.evidence: Figure 19 reports linear-probe curves after 16 ResNet50 residual activations and says early layers plateau quickly. Intermediate CNN outputs are spatial tensors, yet neither the main text nor Appendix E defines whether a 'neuron' is a channel, one channel-location element, or a pooled feature, nor how spatial activations are converted to the probe vector. The appendix gives labels such as layerX.Y.act3 but no pooling, masking, dimensionality, or compute protocol.

key_findings.claim: A pre-existing NeurIPS paper is a closer antecedent than the related-work section acknowledges and materially narrows novelty.
key_findings.evidence: The paper says Dalvi et al.'s NLP feature-selection study is closest. Yet Doimo et al., arXiv 2021 and NeurIPS 2022, already select random chunks of neurons from final hidden representations, study a critical width, test CNNs including ResNet50 on ImageNet, and report that wide representations form redundant clones with chunk error scaling. The present paper adds frozen pre-trained transfer tasks, CKA, adversarial/upstream-loss comparisons, MRL and class-disparity analysis, but the central random-subset and width-threshold phenomenon is not new.

key_findings.claim: The harder-task appendix usefully shows that random-coordinate curves are not confined to small VTAB subsets, while remaining limited to classification with frozen vision encoders.
key_findings.evidence: Figure 20 reports smooth retained-coordinate curves for ImageNet-1k, ImageNetV2, and Places365 under standard and l2-robust ResNet50 encoders, and the ImageNet-to-ImageNetV2 accuracy gap remains visible as coordinates are removed. The evaluation does not cover detection, segmentation, retrieval, calibration, generative tasks, full fine-tuning, distribution shifts beyond ImageNetV2, or nonvision modalities, so claims about broad downstream generality should retain the linear-classification qualifier.

method.core_idea: Treat representation coordinates as a population that can be randomly subsampled, retrain only a downstream linear head on each subset, and define redundancy by the smallest random subset whose average task score remains near the full representation.
method.mechanism: For frozen pre-trained encoders, sample coordinate masks at several retained fractions, train independent linear probes on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, Flowers, Oxford-IIIT-Pets, and selected harder datasets, and compare part-versus-whole linear CKA and transfer accuracy. Summarize each curve with the DR threshold score, compare random coordinates with PCA, dense random projections, MRL prefixes, widths, upstream datasets and losses, and track Gini/CV of class-wise accuracies as coordinates are removed.
assumptions: Linear-probe accuracy captures the downstream information relevant to the intended transfer setting.
Five random masks per retained size adequately estimate the exponential mask average and its variability.
A high mean and small observed standard deviation imply that many, rather than merely some, random subsets succeed.
Linear CKA between contained or overlapping coordinate sets diagnoses replicated information rather than generic anisotropy or low effective rank.
Comparable probe accuracy after top-PCA projection indicates comparable retained variance.
The same probe optimizer and regularization permit fair comparisons across coordinate, PCA, and dense random-projection parameterizations.
Downloaded single checkpoints represent their architecture, upstream dataset, and loss families.
Relative performance T(masked g)/T(g) is comparable when full-layer accuracies differ across architectures and widths.
Class-wise accuracy inequality is a meaningful proxy for fairness even without protected-group attributes.
Selecting representation coordinates translates into practical end-to-end efficiency despite an unchanged frozen backbone.

techniques.role: Measures how frozen-encoder transfer accuracy changes when a linear head receives a random coordinate subset.
Summarizes the smallest retained coordinate fraction whose mean relative task performance reaches a chosen tolerance.
Compares sample geometry induced by a coordinate subset with the complete representation.
Measures similarity and stability between independently drawn coordinate subsets of the same size.
Contrasts random coordinate probes with probes on top and bottom principal-component projections.
Attempts to separate learned coordinate structure from arbitrary linear dimensionality reduction.
Compares architectures, ImageNet-1k versus ImageNet-21k, standard versus adversarial losses, MRL, dropout, and DeCov.
Relates retained-fraction curves to the trained penultimate representation width.
Tracks Gini coefficient and coefficient of variation across label-class accuracies as coordinates are removed.
Extends the coordinate-subset procedure to multiple ResNet residual activations.

evaluations.setting: Standard and l2-adversarial ImageNet-1k ResNet50 penultimate representations transferred to CIFAR-10/100, Flowers, and Oxford-IIIT-Pets.
evaluations.metric: Linear-probe accuracy, DR at selected delta values, part-whole CKA, and standard deviation over five masks.
evaluations.result: Both models tolerate substantial coordinate removal, with the robust model generally retaining accuracy and CKA at smaller fractions; the exact critical fraction is downstream-task dependent.
evaluations.baseline: A separate linear probe on the full 2,048-coordinate representation.

evaluations.setting: Pairs of random subsets and dimensionality-reduction controls on the two ResNet50 representations.
evaluations.metric: Random-pair CKA and downstream accuracy versus retained fraction.
evaluations.result: Random-pair CKA rises rapidly; random coordinates approach top-PCA probe accuracy beyond roughly 20% and outperform the paper's dense random-projection implementation.
evaluations.baseline: Top and bottom principal components plus a column-normalized dense random matrix.

evaluations.setting: Six ImageNet-1k architectures: ViT-S16, ViT-S32, ResNet18, ResNet50, WideResNet50-2, and VGG16.
evaluations.metric: Transfer-accuracy curves and DR at delta=0.9.
evaluations.result: Every architecture displays some random-coordinate redundancy, but discardable fractions span 0.2-0.95 across task/model pairs and are not ordered by representation length alone.
evaluations.baseline: Each model's own full-layer linear-probe score.

evaluations.setting: ViT-S16 and ViT-S32 pretrained on ImageNet-1k versus ImageNet-21k.
evaluations.metric: Transfer accuracy and DR versus retained fraction.
evaluations.result: ImageNet-21k pretraining usually yields more outward curves and higher DR, with effect size varying by downstream task.
evaluations.baseline: Matched architecture pretrained on the smaller upstream dataset.

evaluations.setting: ResNet50 variants with penultimate widths from 8 to 2,048 and a ResNet50 trained with MRL.
evaluations.metric: Relative and absolute transfer accuracy versus coordinate count/fraction, including designated MRL prefixes.
evaluations.result: Narrower trained layers retain less removable capacity; MRL prefixes dominate at the smallest budgets, while random subsets from wide models catch up at larger budgets.
evaluations.baseline: Full representation for each width and the MRL model's explicitly optimized prefix.

evaluations.setting: Nine additional ImageNet-1k ResNet50 models trained with dropout 0.1-0.8 or DeCov coefficient 1e-4.
evaluations.metric: Transfer accuracy and approximate DR curves.
evaluations.result: The displayed curves are qualitatively similar across regularizer settings, which the paper interprets as little effect on diffused redundancy.
evaluations.baseline: Ordinary cross-entropy ResNet50, without upstream-seed uncertainty or a measured decorrelation check.

evaluations.setting: Coordinate removal on the four main tasks, plus intermediate ResNet50 layers and ImageNet-1k/ImageNetV2/Places365.
evaluations.metric: Gini and coefficient of variation of class accuracies, per-class accuracy heatmaps, and linear-probe accuracy curves.
evaluations.result: Class-accuracy dispersion increases as mean accuracy falls; early and late layers and the harder classification datasets all show rapid performance gains with additional coordinates.
evaluations.baseline: The complete representation at each evaluated layer and model.

limitations: The DR estimator uses only five masks per tested size and reports neither mask-success probabilities nor confidence bounds on the critical retained fraction.
Equation 1 averages performance, so it does not formalize the stronger narrative that any or almost every random subset succeeds.
The retained-fraction grid is discrete and no interpolation, monotonicity correction, or threshold-selection uncertainty is reported.
CKA between a subset and its parent representation is not an independent test and cannot identify literal feature replication without null and causal controls.
Top-PCA probe accuracy is not retained variance, so the stated maximum-variation explanation is unsupported by the reported observable.

The released random-projection code uses a positive uniform matrix rather than the Gaussian matrix described in the paper; at full dimension the observed accuracy gap should vanish under a well-conditioned invertible transform.
Most architecture/loss conclusions are based on one downloaded pre-trained checkpoint rather than independent upstream training seeds.
The newly trained dropout and DeCov models lack upstream optimization details, checkpoint accuracies, seed replication, and evidence that DeCov changed the evaluated covariance.
The width study changes the trained representation and full-layer target and does not provide a matched causal width-by-training design.
The intermediate-layer experiment does not define the neuron unit, spatial pooling, tensor masking, or dimensionality for convolutional activations.
The main evidence is frozen linear classification on vision datasets; detection, segmentation, retrieval, generation, nonlinear heads, full fine-tuning, language, and audio are absent.
No end-to-end latency, FLOPs, memory, energy, or deployment experiment shows that random-coordinate probing removes backbone computation.
Gini and CV are over label-class accuracies rather than protected groups; the fairness framing lacks a normative target and subgroup metadata.
The appendix heatmaps contain class accuracies, not prediction distributions, so they do not validate the stated homogenization of predictions.
The closest direct random-chunk/critical-width predecessor, Doimo et al. (NeurIPS 2022), is absent from the related-work and novelty discussion.
There are minor reproducibility errors and ambiguities, including 'CIFAR10/1000' on page 7 and no exact seed/split accounting for every plotted checkpoint.
failure_modes: A high mean over masks hides a small but operationally important tail of coordinate subsets that fail badly.
A low-rank or anisotropic representation yields high CKA for random subsets even though coordinates do not contain exchangeable copies of semantic features.
Task signal lies in a low-variance direction, causing PCA accuracy and variance-retention interpretations to diverge.
A nonzero-mean, ill-conditioned random projection makes the dense-projection baseline look artificially weak even at full dimension.
The retained coordinates save probe parameters but the full encoder and penultimate computation remain necessary, eliminating claimed runtime or energy savings.
A new downstream task relies on a rare specialized coordinate and falls outside the four-task average trend.
Relative accuracy thresholds make a weak full representation appear highly redundant or obscure absolute quality differences across models.
Coordinate removal disproportionately damages a few classes, subpopulations, or rare examples despite a small aggregate accuracy change.
Class-accuracy inequality is mistaken for demographic fairness, leading to mitigation choices that do not address real protected-group harms.
A single checkpoint's redundancy is attributed to an architecture or loss even though upstream seed and optimization variability dominate.
Randomly selecting coordinates from an intermediate convolutional tensor changes spatial information or channel semantics in an implementation-specific way.
Features are stored in superposition: random subsets preserve probe accuracy but individual neurons cannot be interpreted as replicated concepts.
reusable_insights: Define redundancy operationally as a distribution over subset outcomes: report mean, lower quantiles, worst-case masks, and confidence intervals separately.
Separate coordinate redundancy, low effective rank, semantic feature replication, and task sufficiency; each needs a different diagnostic.
At full dimension, any invertible linear transform must preserve optimal linear-probe expressivity; use this as a mandatory sanity check for projection baselines.
Use zero-mean isotropic or orthogonal random projections and retune regularization or whiten features before interpreting optimization gaps as information gaps.
Compare random coordinate subsets against effective-rank predictions, whitened controls, leverage-score sampling, sparse probing, PCA, and learned nested prefixes.
Measure both relative and absolute downstream performance when comparing representation widths or architectures.
Efficiency claims require an executable path from representation sparsity to skipped operators, plus measured latency, memory traffic, energy, and hardware utilization.
Treat class-level disparity as a diagnostic rather than fairness itself; add protected-group evaluation and matched-accuracy controls where fairness is claimed.
Repeat upstream pre-training seeds when assigning redundancy differences to losses, regularizers, datasets, or architectures.
A random-subset curve is a useful representation fingerprint and can be modeled jointly with width, effective rank, target alignment, and mask variance.
open_questions: Does diffused redundancy persist after whitening, when CKA's covariance-spectrum shortcut is removed?
What fraction of masks clears a task threshold with high confidence, and how does that tail probability scale with width and task difficulty?
Can random-subset accuracy curves be predicted from effective rank, leverage scores, neural-collapse geometry, or the clone model of Doimo et al.?
Which mechanism dominates: replicated noisy clones, low-rank class structure, polysemantic superposition, or optimization-induced coordinate exchangeability?
Does a corrected orthogonal/Gaussian random-projection baseline match or beat coordinate sampling after optimizer and regularization retuning?
Can a compiler or structurally pruned head skip the corresponding penultimate and upstream computation and deliver real wall-clock savings?
How stable are DR thresholds across pre-training seeds, model checkpoints, downstream sample sizes, and label noise?
Do nonlinear probes, detection, segmentation, retrieval, generative tasks, language models, and full fine-tuning preserve the same subset curves?
Can task-conditioned masks improve the Pareto frontier while retaining strong lower-tail guarantees for unseen tasks?
How should coordinate-removal systems optimize worst-class and protected-group outcomes at a fixed aggregate accuracy and hardware budget?
What exactly constitutes a neuron in convolutional feature maps, and do channel-, location-, and activation-level masks behave differently?
Does orthogonal regularization or explicit effective-rank control causally change diffused redundancy under a fully replicated pre-training study?

competitive_landscape.title: Redundant representations help generalization in wide neural networks
competitive_landscape.difference: Doimo et al. already analyze random chunks of final hidden neurons, a critical layer width, CNNs including ResNet50/ImageNet, and a clone/noise mechanism with chunk-error scaling. The reviewed paper's main additions are pre-trained transfer across tasks, CKA, upstream-loss/dataset comparisons, MRL, and class-disparity analysis; describing the NLP selection paper as closest materially overstates novelty.

competitive_landscape.title: Analyzing Redundancy in Pretrained Transformer Models
competitive_landscape.difference: Dalvi et al. select task-relevant neurons across BERT and XLNet layers and retain 97% performance with at most 10% of neurons. Their subsets are optimized and span layers, whereas the reviewed paper's distinctive test is unoptimized random coordinates within one vision layer.

competitive_landscape.title: Matryoshka Representation Learning
competitive_landscape.difference: MRL deliberately orders information into nested prefixes and reports embedding-size and real retrieval-speed gains across modalities. The reviewed paper shows natural random-coordinate sufficiency in ordinary and MRL models but does not match MRL's known prefix, deployability, or measured systems benefit at extreme low dimensions.

competitive_landscape.title: RankMe: Assessing the downstream performance of pretrained self-supervised representations by their rank
competitive_landscape.difference: RankMe uses effective rank as an unsupervised predictor of downstream representation quality across hundreds of SSL training episodes. It supplies the spectral control missing from the reviewed study: random-subset curves should be tested against effective-rank and collapse explanations before being interpreted as coordinate-wise copies.

competitive_landscape.title: Finding Neurons in a Haystack: Case Studies with Sparse Probing
competitive_landscape.difference: Gurnee et al. use k-sparse probes across seven language models and more than 100 features to distinguish dedicated neurons, sparse combinations, and superposition. Their optimized feature-specific sparsity complements the reviewed paper's random task-level sufficiency and shows why probe accuracy alone cannot identify replicated semantic units.
competitive_landscape.source_version: arXiv:2305.01610v2 (2023-06-02); v1 preceded the reviewed paper

competitive_landscape.title: Toy Models of Superposition
competitive_landscape.difference: Elhage et al. model how more sparse features than neurons can be stored in superposition, making neurons polysemantic rather than replicated. The reviewed paper cites it but does not experimentally distinguish superposition from its language of features diffused redundantly across neurons.

competitive_landscape.title: Barlow Twins: Self-Supervised Learning via Redundancy Reduction
competitive_landscape.difference: Barlow Twins explicitly drives cross-coordinate correlations toward identity while finding that high-dimensional embeddings help downstream performance. Its redundancy notion is pairwise correlation rather than random-subset task sufficiency, underscoring that the reviewed paper must measure whether DeCov actually changed coordinate dependence before claiming decorrelation has no effect.

competitive_landscape.title: Preventing Dimensional Collapse in Self-Supervised Learning via Orthogonality Regularization
competitive_landscape.difference: He et al. apply orthogonality across encoder weights and evaluate weight, hidden-feature, and representation eigenspectra on CNNs and Transformers, reporting transfer gains. This is a stronger causal and spectral test of redundancy/collapse than the reviewed paper's one-coefficient DeCov curve without confirmation that the target layer was decorrelated.

competitive_landscape.title: Once-for-All: Train One Network and Specialize it for Efficient Deployment
competitive_landscape.difference: OFA trains nested depth, width, kernel, and resolution choices and selects hardware-specific subnetworks with measured device latency. The reviewed approach avoids special upstream training but only reduces a frozen linear probe's input, so its claimed energy and inference benefits are not comparable until skipped backbone computation is demonstrated.

competitive_landscape.title: SLEB: Streamlining LLMs through Redundancy Verification and Elimination of Transformer Blocks
competitive_landscape.difference: SLEB identifies redundant blocks and removes executable computation, reporting actual LLM inference acceleration while preserving perplexity and accuracy. It operates at a different granularity and modality, but it illustrates the systems evidence required to turn representation similarity into an efficiency claim.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: Wide pre-trained representations contain redundancy diffused across coordinates, so many random subsets above a task-specific critical mass resemble and transfer nearly as well as the whole; upstream training controls this frontier and coordinate removal may enable efficient transfer with class-level tradeoffs.
novelty_assessment.evidence: The paper provides a substantial cross-model collection of random-subset linear-probe and CKA curves, compares standard/adversarial training, ImageNet-1k/21k, architecture, trained width, MRL, dropout and DeCov, and checks class-accuracy dispersion and harder vision datasets. These experiments make task-conditioned random-coordinate sufficiency a useful empirical representation diagnostic.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: The empirical atlas of frozen pre-trained transfer settings is valuable, but the central phenomenon and critical-width story were already demonstrated more directly by Doimo et al. before this work. Several mechanistic and practical claims are not supported: PCA accuracy is misread as variance capture, the released dense-projection baseline uses a positive uniform matrix and fails an invertible full-dimension sanity check, five masks do not establish high-probability success, class disparity is not demographic fairness, and no end-to-end efficiency is measured. The strongest defensible contribution is the broad comparative characterization of random-coordinate linear-probe sufficiency, not a new discovery of redundancy or a validated deployment method.

reviewer_notes: Read all 25 extracted pages and directly inspected the final NeurIPS PDF at high resolution, including Table 1, Figures 1-22, rotated class-accuracy heatmaps, DR plots, intermediate-layer plots, and the dropout/DeCov appendix. Audited Equation 1, all sampling counts, CKA/PCA interpretations, width and MRL comparisons, class-disparity language, probe training details, and systems claims. The official code repository was checked on 2026-08-23: its parent repository pins deep-learning-base commit 3c0e3dd3fbb484b00efd6914b4afd349db0563a6, whose randproj path uses F.normalize(torch.rand((in_fts,in_fts)), dim=0), not the zero-mean Gaussian projection described on page 7. Ten primary arXiv/proceedings competitors were checked at the exact versions recorded above; the most material novelty audit is the omitted arXiv:2106.03485/NeurIPS 2022 direct predecessor. No projections were rebuilt.
